title: Adult sleep duration recommendations
content: For adults aged 18 to 60, CDC recommends at least seven hours of sleep each day. Repeated shorter nights are a reason to review the time available for sleep, rather than diagnose a disorder.
source_locator: Getting enough sleep; adult age table
support_anchor: 7 or more hours
observable_conditions: Sleep duration below the age-specific recommendation
required_context: Age band compatible with 18 to 60 years
non_applicable_conditions: Age under 18 or above 60

title: Sleep duration in later middle age
content: CDC recommends seven to nine hours of daily sleep for adults aged 61 to 64. The relevant age group must be known before this range is applied to a sleep record.
source_locator: Getting enough sleep; adult age table
observable_conditions: Daily sleep duration is available
non_applicable_conditions: Other age groups

title: Sleep duration recommendations for older adults
content: For adults aged 65 and older, CDC lists seven to eight hours of sleep each day. This age-specific range differs from the recommendation for younger adults.
source_locator: Getting enough sleep; adult age table
support_anchor: 65 years and older
observable_conditions: Daily sleep duration is available
non_applicable_conditions: Age below 65

title: Teenagers have a different sleep recommendation
content: CDC recommends eight to ten hours of daily sleep for teenagers aged 13 to 17. An adult sleep target should not be transferred to this age group.
source_locator: Getting enough sleep; teenager age table
observable_conditions: Daily sleep duration is available
non_applicable_conditions: Adults

title: Protect time for sleep in a busy schedule
content: Busy schedules can squeeze out sleep. NHLBI advises setting aside enough time for sleep to protect health and daytime functioning.
support_anchor: Sleep is often the first thing that busy people squeeze out of their schedules
observable_conditions: Repeatedly shortened sleep opportunity or sleep duration
required_context: A schedule constraint is needed to attribute the shortage to busyness
non_applicable_conditions: No evidence of insufficient sleep

title: A familiar short sleep routine is not proof of adaptation
content: NHLBI rejects the idea that people can learn to thrive on little sleep without adverse effects. A stable short routine does not by itself establish that sleep needs are met.
source_locator: Final paragraph about a common myth
support_anchor: people can learn to get by on little sleep
observable_conditions: Sleep is consistently short even without a new decline
non_applicable_conditions: Sleep duration is sufficient for the applicable age group

title: Hours slept and sleep quality are different
content: Sleep quality concerns uninterrupted, refreshing sleep as well as duration. CDC lists difficulty falling asleep, repeated awakenings, and tiredness despite enough sleep as possible quality concerns. Recorded hours alone do not establish sleep quality.
support_anchor: uninterrupted and refreshing sleep
observable_conditions: Sleep duration is recorded but sleep quality may be unknown
required_context: Sleep-onset difficulty, awakenings, or subjective refreshment to establish a particular poor-quality concern
non_applicable_conditions: A claim that duration alone proves quality

title: Night awakenings are a separate sleep concern
content: CDC lists repeated night awakenings among signs of poor sleep quality. Total duration alone does not indicate whether repeated awakenings occurred.
support_anchor: Repeatedly waking up during the night
observable_conditions: Repeated awakenings are documented
required_context: Awakening history or measured sleep continuity
non_applicable_conditions: Only duration and sleep start or end are available

title: Long night-time sleep without feeling rested needs context
content: NHLBI advises discussing sleep with a doctor when someone sleeps more than eight hours a night but still does not feel rested. Feeling unrefreshed must be reported; it cannot be inferred from night-time sleep duration.
source_locator: Who is at risk; final advice
support_anchor: don't feel well rested
observable_conditions: More than eight hours of night-time sleep with reported lack of refreshment
required_context: Subjective lack of refreshment and night-time sleep duration
non_applicable_conditions: No information about feeling rested

title: Sleep supports learning and attention
content: Adequate sleep helps learning, attention, and problem solving. Repeated sleep restriction is worth reviewing, but a wearable record alone does not establish impaired cognition in an individual.
support_anchor: improves learning and problem-solving skills
observable_conditions: Repeatedly shortened sleep
required_context: Symptoms are needed to claim actual cognitive impairment
non_applicable_conditions: Diagnosing impairment from wearable data alone

title: Several short nights can affect daytime performance
content: NHLBI describes slower reactions and more mistakes after repeated sleep loss. Several shortened nights may deserve attention even when a person believes they function well.
support_anchor: After several nights of losing sleep
observable_conditions: Several nights of reduced sleep duration
required_context: Actual performance or symptoms are needed to claim individual impairment
non_applicable_conditions: No repeated sleep restriction

title: Ongoing sleep deficiency and immune function
content: NHLBI explains that ongoing sleep deficiency can alter the body's response to germs. This general benefit of adequate sleep does not allow a wearable record to diagnose infection.
support_anchor: body’s ability to fight germs and sickness
observable_conditions: Ongoing insufficient sleep
non_applicable_conditions: Inferring an infection from sleep or heart-rate changes

title: Sleep is involved in appetite regulation
content: NHLBI explains that insufficient sleep can affect hormones involved in hunger and fullness. Individual appetite change requires separate evidence rather than being inferred from sleep duration.
support_anchor: hormones that make you feel hungry
observable_conditions: Repeated insufficient sleep
required_context: Food intake or appetite information for individual claims
non_applicable_conditions: Diagnosing a metabolic disorder from wearable observations

title: Do not drive when sleepy
content: NHS advises avoiding driving when sleepy. This safety advice depends on actual sleepiness and a driving context, which sleep duration measurements do not automatically establish.
source_locator: How you can treat insomnia yourself; Don't
support_anchor: do not drive when you feel sleepy
observable_conditions: Reported sleepiness
non_applicable_conditions: Sleepiness or driving context unknown

title: Sleep needs vary between people
content: NHS notes that sleep requirements vary among people, with adults averaging seven to nine hours. Duration should be considered alongside individual experience rather than treated as a diagnosis.
support_anchor: Everyone needs different amounts of sleep
observable_conditions: Adult sleep duration is being reviewed
required_context: Individual sleep experience to assess adequacy
non_applicable_conditions: Using one duration target as a diagnostic test

title: Persistent insomnia symptoms can warrant professional review
content: On its insomnia page, NHS advises seeing a GP if changing sleeping habits has not helped insomnia, if sleeping difficulties have lasted months, or if insomnia makes daily life difficult to cope with. A two-week wearable window alone cannot establish these conditions.
source_locator: Non-urgent advice: See a GP if
support_anchor: you've had trouble sleeping for months
observable_conditions: Reported sleeping difficulties or insomnia symptoms
required_context: Months-long sleeping difficulties, or insomnia with failed habit changes or substantial daily-life impact
non_applicable_conditions: Only a brief duration record without reported problems

title: Keep bedtime and waking time consistent
content: NHLBI recommends going to bed and waking at the same times each day. Changing sleep times repeatedly is a reason to review routine consistency, independently of total sleep hours.
support_anchor: Go to bed and wake up at the same time every day
observable_conditions: Repeated variability in bedtime or wake time
non_applicable_conditions: A stable schedule alone does not establish a problem

title: For sleeping difficulties, get up at a consistent time
content: For people with insomnia, NHS advises waking and getting out of bed at the same time each day. This targeted advice requires sleeping difficulties rather than merely a late but stable schedule.
source_locator: How you can treat insomnia yourself; Do
support_anchor: wake up and get out of bed at the same time every day
observable_conditions: Inconsistent wake time with reported sleeping difficulties
non_applicable_conditions: No evidence of insomnia symptoms

title: Limit weeknight and weekend schedule differences
content: NHLBI advises keeping weeknight and weekend sleep schedules similar, with differences around an hour or less. Sleeping much later on weekends can disturb the sleep-wake rhythm.
support_anchor: Limit the difference to no more than about an hour
observable_conditions: Bedtime or wake time differs substantially between weekdays and weekends
required_context: Calendar grouping does not itself establish workdays
non_applicable_conditions: Weekday and weekend sleep times are similar

title: Reserve quiet time before bedtime
content: NHLBI recommends using the hour before bedtime for quiet activities. A bedtime record can identify when this period would fall, but does not reveal what someone did then.
support_anchor: Use the hour before bed for quiet time
observable_conditions: Bedtime routine is being reviewed
required_context: Information about pre-bed activities for targeted advice
non_applicable_conditions: Assuming a missing bedtime routine from timestamps alone

title: Bright screens before bed can interfere with sleep
content: NHLBI recommends avoiding bright artificial light before bedtime because it can signal wakefulness. Screen exposure must be known before attributing sleep timing changes to screens.
support_anchor: bright artificial light
observable_conditions: Known bright-screen exposure shortly before bed
non_applicable_conditions: Exposure is unknown

title: Late caffeine can have lasting effects
content: NHLBI notes that caffeine's effects can last up to eight hours and late-afternoon coffee may hinder falling asleep. Timing and amount of caffeine intake require separate records.
support_anchor: effects of caffeine can last up to 8 hours
observable_conditions: Known afternoon or evening caffeine use with sleeping difficulty
non_applicable_conditions: No caffeine history

title: Avoid heavy meals near bedtime
content: NHLBI advises avoiding heavy or large meals in the hours before bed; a light snack is acceptable. Sleep timing data alone does not show meal timing or meal size.
support_anchor: Avoid heavy or large meals
observable_conditions: Known large meal shortly before bed
non_applicable_conditions: Meal information unknown

title: Alcohol before bed is a separate habit to review
content: NHLBI recommends avoiding alcohol before bedtime. A wearable sleep change does not establish that alcohol was consumed, so this advice needs a drinking history.
support_anchor: avoid alcoholic drinks before bed
observable_conditions: Alcohol use near bedtime is reported
non_applicable_conditions: Alcohol exposure is unknown

title: Nicotine is a stimulant that may interfere with sleep
content: NHLBI identifies nicotine as a stimulant that can interfere with sleep. Smoking or other nicotine use must be established before linking this habit to a changed sleep pattern.
support_anchor: Nicotine and caffeine are stimulants
observable_conditions: Nicotine use with sleep concerns
non_applicable_conditions: Nicotine use unknown

title: A quiet, cool, dark bedroom supports sleep
content: NHLBI advises maintaining a quiet, cool, dark bedroom. Wearable times and durations do not establish bedroom temperature, light, or noise conditions.
support_anchor: Keep your bedroom quiet, cool, and dark
observable_conditions: Known disruptive bedroom environment
non_applicable_conditions: Environment unknown

title: Relaxation can be part of a bedtime routine
content: NHLBI suggests a hot bath or relaxation techniques before bed. These are optional routine practices, rather than an explanation for an unexplained timing shift.
support_anchor: use relaxation techniques before bed
observable_conditions: A pre-bed routine is under consideration
required_context: Reported difficulty relaxing or a request for routine options
non_applicable_conditions: Inferring stress or anxiety from wearable signals

title: Keep adult naps short and consider their timing
content: NHLBI recommends adult naps of no more than twenty minutes. Separately, for people who have difficulty falling asleep at night, it advises limiting naps or taking them earlier in the afternoon.
support_anchor: Adults should nap for no more than 20 minutes
observable_conditions: Adult naps are recorded or reported
required_context: Nap duration for the general length advice; night-time sleep-onset difficulty for the timing advice
non_applicable_conditions: Nap history is unknown

title: Changing shifts can make sleep adjustment harder
content: For shift workers, NHLBI suggests limiting shift changes to allow the body clock to adjust. Variable sleep times alone do not prove that someone works rotating shifts.
support_anchor: Limit shift changes so your body clock can adjust
observable_conditions: Changing work shifts and disrupted sleep schedule
non_applicable_conditions: Shift work unknown

title: Bright work lighting is specific to shift workers
content: NHLBI suggests keeping workplace lighting bright for shift workers. This is work-context advice and should not be confused with avoiding bright light just before bedtime.
support_anchor: Keep the lights bright at work
observable_conditions: Shift work is established
non_applicable_conditions: No confirmed shift work

title: Limit shift-work caffeine to the early part of the shift
content: NHLBI advises shift workers to limit caffeine to the first part of their shift. This recommendation depends on work and caffeine timing, not simply a late recorded bedtime.
support_anchor: Limit caffeine use to the first part of your shift
observable_conditions: Shift worker using caffeine
non_applicable_conditions: Shift work or caffeine use unknown

title: Reduce light and sound during daytime sleep after shifts
content: For shift workers sleeping during the day, NHLBI suggests removing light and sound distractions, including light-blocking curtains. Daytime sleep and shift work must be confirmed.
support_anchor: Remove sound and light distractions
observable_conditions: Daytime sleep associated with shift work
non_applicable_conditions: Only ordinary overnight sleep is recorded

title: A sleep diary gives a timeline of changes
content: CDC recommends recording bedtimes, night awakenings, waking times, and naps in a sleep diary. This preserves the sequence of changes rather than only a period average.
support_anchor: Your sleep diary should include when you
observable_conditions: A changed or variable sleep pattern needs review
required_context: Awakenings and naps need separate records if absent
non_applicable_conditions: Inventing unrecorded awakenings or naps

title: Repeated lost sleep can accumulate
content: NHLBI explains that regularly getting less sleep than needed adds up over time. The duration and recurrence of shortened nights matter; a current improvement does not quantify a complete recovery.
source_locator: Sleep loss paragraph following age table
support_anchor: the sleep loss adds up
observable_conditions: Several shortened nights rather than a single isolated reading
non_applicable_conditions: Claiming a fixed number of recovery nights

title: More sleep on days off can signal insufficient workday sleep
content: NHLBI notes that sleeping more on days off may indicate insufficient sleep on workdays. Extra sleep may feel helpful but can also disrupt the sleep-wake rhythm.
support_anchor: Sleeping more on days off might be a sign
observable_conditions: Longer sleep and later timing on days off
non_applicable_conditions: Assuming every weekend is a day off

title: A nap is not a substitute for night-time sleep
content: NHLBI states that naps can briefly improve alertness but do not provide all benefits of night-time sleep. A nap should not be treated as proof that lost sleep was fully compensated.
support_anchor: napping doesn't supply all the other benefits of nighttime sleep
observable_conditions: Napping after shortened night-time sleep
non_applicable_conditions: No nap information

title: Keep regular hours after a bad night
content: For people experiencing insomnia, NHS advises sticking to regular sleeping hours rather than sleeping in after a bad night. A resolved short episode does not itself prove insomnia.
source_locator: How you can treat insomnia yourself; Don't
support_anchor: do not sleep in after a bad night's sleep
observable_conditions: Recent bad night and sleeping difficulties
required_context: Reported bad sleep or insomnia symptoms
non_applicable_conditions: Only a device estimate without reported sleeping difficulty

title: Insomnia duration categories require a symptom history
content: NHS distinguishes short-term insomnia lasting under three months from long-term insomnia lasting at least three months. The distinction requires a symptom history, not just fourteen days of short sleep estimates.
support_anchor: less than 3 months
observable_conditions: Reported sleeping difficulties with known duration
non_applicable_conditions: Diagnosing insomnia from estimated sleep hours

title: Travel-related sleep changes require a travel history
content: NHS describes jet lag as a disturbed sleep pattern after a long flight and generally advises adapting to the destination time zone. For a short trip of two to three days it offers keeping original eating and sleeping times as an alternative. A timing change alone does not establish jet lag.
source_locator: Introduction, After you arrive, and Short trips
support_anchor: change your sleep schedule to the new time zone
observable_conditions: Sleep timing changed after a long flight across time zones
required_context: Confirmed travel, destination time zone, and trip duration
non_applicable_conditions: No travel history; applying destination-time advice unconditionally to a short trip

title: Short trips have different sleep schedule considerations
content: For trips lasting two to three days, NHS says travellers could keep their original eating and sleeping times to avoid another adjustment on return. This advice is specific to a known short trip.
support_anchor: If your trip is short
observable_conditions: A short trip across time zones is planned
non_applicable_conditions: Travel context unknown

title: Some activity is better than none
content: CDC advises adults to move more and sit less. Any amount of moderate or vigorous activity provides some benefit, even before recommended weekly amounts are reached.
support_anchor: Some physical activity is better than none
observable_conditions: Low or declining movement gives an opportunity to add activity
required_context: Intensity information is needed to count recommended aerobic minutes
non_applicable_conditions: Equating steps directly with guideline compliance

title: Build up activity gradually after inactivity
content: MedlinePlus advises people who have been inactive to start slowly and add more exercise gradually. Small increases can be useful without demanding an abrupt jump in activity.
support_anchor: If you have been inactive
observable_conditions: Recently low or reduced physical activity
required_context: Health and mobility context for exercise prescription
non_applicable_conditions: Prescribing an intense programme from wearable data alone

title: Moderate-intensity aerobic activity has a weekly target
content: CDC recommends at least 150 minutes of moderate-intensity aerobic activity per week for adults. Device moving minutes and steps are insufficient to determine whether that intensity requirement is met.
support_anchor: 150 minutes of moderate-intensity physical activity a week
observable_conditions: Moderate-intensity aerobic minutes are documented
non_applicable_conditions: Only steps or unspecified active minutes are available

title: Vigorous activity uses a different weekly duration target
content: CDC lists 75 minutes of vigorous aerobic activity per week as an adult option. Applying it requires actual vigorous activity; total movement time cannot be assumed to have that intensity.
support_anchor: 75 minutes of vigorous-intensity
observable_conditions: Vigorous aerobic activity is documented
non_applicable_conditions: Intensity unknown

title: Split activity into manageable portions
content: CDC explains that adults can spread activity across the week and divide it into smaller chunks. A single continuous exercise session is not required to accumulate aerobic activity.
support_anchor: break it up into smaller chunks of time
observable_conditions: Reduced activity or limited opportunities for long sessions
required_context: Intensity is required for counting guideline minutes
non_applicable_conditions: Assuming every recorded active minute is moderate intensity

title: Muscle strengthening is distinct from walking totals
content: CDC recommends muscle-strengthening activity on at least two days each week that works all major muscle groups. Step counts do not show whether this separate activity took place or which muscle groups it involved.
source_locator: Recommendations for adults and muscle-strengthening example
support_anchor: at least 2 days of muscle-strengthening activity
observable_conditions: A strengthening routine is being reviewed
required_context: Strengthening activity records including days and muscle groups
non_applicable_conditions: Only step or generic movement counts are available

title: Additional aerobic activity can add benefits
content: CDC notes that activity beyond the minimum weekly moderate or vigorous amounts can offer further health benefits. This assessment requires known intensity and does not follow from steps alone.
support_anchor: gain even more health benefits
observable_conditions: Documented aerobic activity already reaches the adult guideline
non_applicable_conditions: Unknown intensity or unverified guideline attainment

title: Relative intensity depends on fitness
content: CDC explains that the same activity can be vigorous for one person and moderate for a fitter person. Activity intensity cannot be assigned solely from a daily movement total.
support_anchor: may only be moderate for a very fit person
observable_conditions: Activity intensity needs interpretation
non_applicable_conditions: Inferring intensity from steps alone

title: The talk test helps describe aerobic activity effort
content: For aerobic activity, CDC's talk test describes moderate intensity as allowing conversation but not singing; vigorous intensity permits only a few words before pausing for breath. This requires observed effort, not just active minutes.
support_anchor: can talk, but not sing
observable_conditions: Effort during aerobic activity is being assessed
required_context: An aerobic activity and breathing or talk-test observation
non_applicable_conditions: Effort or aerobic-activity context is unrecorded

title: Step count can miss non-step exercise intensity
content: Google's device documentation notes that steps may not reflect intensity during activities such as spinning or yoga. Lower steps alone therefore do not establish that all physical activity decreased.
support_anchor: step count might not reflect your intensity level
observable_conditions: Steps change while other activity may differ
required_context: Activity type for interpreting non-step exercise
non_applicable_conditions: Concluding intensity or total exercise from steps alone

title: Walking can become part of an everyday routine
content: NHS suggests incorporating activity into everyday life, including walking or cycling instead of using a car. Routine opportunities may help restore activity when daily movement has declined.
support_anchor: make activity part of everyday life
observable_conditions: Low or declining routine movement
required_context: Mobility and transport context for specific options
non_applicable_conditions: Assuming everyone can safely walk or cycle

title: Choose activities that fit preferences and available times
content: CDC recommends starting with activities, locations, and times a person enjoys. When discussing an activity plan, preferences and available times can help identify suitable options beyond a numeric step goal.
support_anchor: Start with activities, locations, and times you enjoy
observable_conditions: Activity habit is low or difficult to maintain
required_context: Personal preferences and availability for choosing individualized options
non_applicable_conditions: Prescribing an unsuitable activity without context

title: Social activity can support motivation
content: CDC suggests being active with others for motivation and encouragement. This is an option for someone seeking support, rather than an explanation for an observed activity decline.
support_anchor: Try activities with others for motivation
observable_conditions: A person wants support maintaining activity
required_context: Social preferences or reported motivational barrier
non_applicable_conditions: No evidence of a motivational or social barrier

title: Use an activity diary to find time opportunities
content: When lack of time is a barrier, CDC suggests monitoring daily activities for one week with a diary. The diary can reveal usable activity periods that a daily movement total does not identify.
source_locator: Ways to overcome obstacles; I don't have time
support_anchor: Monitor your daily activities for 1 week
observable_conditions: Low activity with a reported time barrier
required_context: Actual daily schedule and time barrier
non_applicable_conditions: Assuming a time barrier from low steps

title: Put planned activity on the calendar
content: CDC recommends writing physical activity on the calendar when other demands crowd it out. This supports habit maintenance but requires knowledge of the person's schedule.
source_locator: Ways to overcome obstacles; I have so much to do already
support_anchor: writing it on your calendar
observable_conditions: Reported competing demands reduce activity
non_applicable_conditions: Schedule reason is unknown

title: Health conditions change activity planning
content: MedlinePlus advises people with chronic health problems or special health needs to ask their provider about appropriate activity types and amounts. Wearable movement data does not supply this medical context.
source_locator: Older adults, pregnant women, and people with chronic health problems
support_anchor: people who have disabilities or special health needs
observable_conditions: A chronic condition, disability, or special need is established
required_context: Relevant health condition and activity safety history
non_applicable_conditions: Medical or disability context unknown

title: Interrupt long periods of not moving
content: NHS recommends reducing time sitting or lying down and interrupting long periods without movement with some activity. This concerns continuous periods as well as the total time accumulated across a day.
source_locator: Adults should aim to; sitting and movement bullet
support_anchor: break up long periods of not moving with some activity
observable_conditions: Long uninterrupted daytime low-movement intervals with adequate wear coverage
required_context: Mobility and posture context for an individual sitting claim
non_applicable_conditions: Low movement due to non-wear or sleep

title: Exercise does not make prolonged sitting irrelevant
content: NHS explains that meeting a weekly activity target does not remove all concerns about spending the remaining time sitting or lying down. Exercise and prolonged sitting are separate behaviours to review.
support_anchor: hit your weekly activity target
observable_conditions: Recorded activity coexists with substantial low-movement periods
required_context: Sitting posture and known activity intensity for guideline claims
non_applicable_conditions: Assuming low-movement estimates prove sitting

title: Reduce sitting across the whole day
content: NHS recommends reducing sitting time as well as increasing activity. Total time sitting remains relevant even if it is spread across several parts of the day.
support_anchor: reduce the amount of time you and your family spend sitting down
observable_conditions: Substantial or increasing daily low movement
required_context: Confirmed sitting for a specific sedentary-time conclusion
non_applicable_conditions: Non-wear is recorded as no movement

title: Commuting offers opportunities to sit less
content: MyHealth London suggests standing for some of a journey or walking part of a bus trip. This option depends on safe transport and mobility conditions.
source_locator: Stand instead of sitting when you travel
support_anchor: get off the bus a few stops early and walk
observable_conditions: Sedentary commuting is established
non_applicable_conditions: Commute unknown

title: Walking to a colleague can interrupt desk sitting
content: MyHealth London suggests walking to speak with a colleague rather than sending an email. This is a workplace movement option for people whose work involves prolonged sitting.
support_anchor: Go over to talk to colleagues rather than sending them an email
observable_conditions: Desk work with prolonged sitting
required_context: Workplace layout and ability to walk
non_applicable_conditions: Work context unknown

title: Consider standing or walking meetings
content: MyHealth London lists standing desks and standing or walking meetings as ways to reduce workplace sitting. Suitability depends on mobility, tasks, and workplace arrangements.
support_anchor: standing or walking meeting
observable_conditions: Meetings or desk work involve prolonged sitting
non_applicable_conditions: No workplace or meeting information

title: Use television breaks as movement opportunities
content: MyHealth London suggests getting up during television advertisement breaks or moving while watching. The advice requires actual screen-related sitting, rather than a low-movement estimate alone.
source_locator: Take regular breaks from screens at home or at work
support_anchor: get up at every ad break
observable_conditions: Prolonged sitting while watching television
non_applicable_conditions: Screen habits unknown

title: Replace some seated leisure with active tasks
content: MyHealth London suggests planning active time when someone often sits, including walking around meals or preparing food. A replacement should fit the person's actual daily routine.
source_locator: Plan in some active time when you are often sitting
support_anchor: Plan in some active time when you are often sitting
observable_conditions: Substantial habitual seated leisure
non_applicable_conditions: No leisure context

title: Movement includes more than formal exercise
content: MedlinePlus defines physical activity as body movement that uses muscles and more energy than resting. Everyday movement can therefore be considered separately from planned exercise sessions.
support_anchor: Physical activity is any body movement
observable_conditions: Low everyday movement despite possible formal exercise
non_applicable_conditions: Counting unobserved or unworn periods as inactivity

title: Lunch breaks can provide daytime walking opportunities
content: CDC suggests adding physical activity to the workday through a lunch-break walk when feasible. A daytime low-movement record does not establish whether a suitable lunch break or walking opportunity is available.
source_locator: Ways to overcome obstacles; workday activity suggestion in the I'm too tired row
support_anchor: walking during your lunch break
observable_conditions: Daytime low movement with known workday lunch-break context
non_applicable_conditions: Unknown workday or lunch-break context

title: Stairs can add incidental movement
content: CDC includes taking stairs when possible as an option to add activity to the workday. This suggestion depends on safe access and ability, not a prescribed step threshold.
support_anchor: taking the stairs when possible
observable_conditions: Low incidental movement with accessible stairs
non_applicable_conditions: Mobility limitations or context unknown

title: Sedentary behaviour requires posture and context
content: NHS describes sedentary behaviour as sitting or lying for long periods, including seated screen use and car travel. A low-movement estimate should not automatically be relabelled as confirmed sitting.
support_anchor: sitting or lying down for long periods
observable_conditions: Low-movement intervals are available without posture measurement
required_context: Posture and waking context to establish sitting
non_applicable_conditions: Treating sleep or non-wear as confirmed sedentary behaviour

title: Regular physical activity can support sleep
content: CDC lists better sleep among immediate benefits of physical activity. This general benefit does not establish that a particular activity caused an individual's subsequent sleep change.
support_anchor: sleep better
observable_conditions: Activity and sleep patterns are available for joint review
non_applicable_conditions: Declaring a causal effect from a few paired observations

title: Daytime activity and outdoor time support a sleep routine
content: NHLBI recommends spending time outdoors when possible and being physically active as part of healthy sleep habits. This is general routine advice rather than evidence about one late workout.
source_locator: Outdoor time and physical activity bullet
support_anchor: Spend time outside every day
observable_conditions: Low daytime activity accompanies a changed sleep routine
required_context: Outdoor access and mobility for a specific plan
non_applicable_conditions: Inferring outdoor exposure from movement counts

title: Review intense exercise immediately before bed
content: NHLBI advises avoiding intense exercise during the hour before bedtime. Recorded late movement is relevant to checking timing, but intensity must be known before applying this intense-exercise advice directly.
support_anchor: Avoid intense exercise
observable_conditions: Activity occurs close to bedtime
required_context: Intensity and actual timing relative to bedtime
non_applicable_conditions: Assuming every late movement interval is intense exercise

title: Exercise timing advice differs when insomnia is present
content: NHS advises people with insomnia to avoid exercise in the four hours before bed. This targeted recommendation requires reported sleeping difficulties; temporal adjacency alone does not establish insomnia or causation.
source_locator: How you can treat insomnia yourself; Don't
support_anchor: do not exercise at least 4 hours before bed
observable_conditions: Exercise near bedtime with reported insomnia symptoms
non_applicable_conditions: Only movement and sleep timestamps are known

title: Record exercise timing alongside sleep timing
content: CDC includes the time of exercise in a sleep diary alongside bedtime and waking time. Recording both helps preserve the temporal context when reviewing sleep changes.
source_locator: Keeping a sleep diary; exercise entry
support_anchor: Exercise
observable_conditions: Activity timing and subsequent sleep are being compared
required_context: Activity intervals are needed for timing comparisons
non_applicable_conditions: Treating same-date daytime activity as exposure before the previous night's sleep

title: Deployed emergency responders should protect sleep time when planning exercise
content: CDC's NIOSH training advises emergency responders while deployed not to cut into sleep time for exercise. This warning concerns competing time demands in that deployment context rather than claiming exercise generally harms sleep.
support_anchor: Do not cut into your sleep time to exercise
observable_conditions: Exercise competes with time available for sleep during deployment
non_applicable_conditions: Emergency-response deployment context unknown; no evidence of competing sleep and activity time

title: Choose activity times when energy is available
content: When tiredness is an obstacle, CDC suggests scheduling activity for times when a person feels energetic. Wearable sleep hours do not establish the person's preferred or highest-energy time.
source_locator: Ways to overcome obstacles; I'm too tired
support_anchor: when you feel energetic
observable_conditions: Reported tiredness limits activity
non_applicable_conditions: No tiredness or energy history

title: A sleep diary should also record substances and medications
content: CDC's sleep diary includes alcohol, caffeine, and medications as well as sleep and exercise. These additional records help avoid assigning every sleep change to an adjacent activity session.
source_locator: Keeping a sleep diary; drinks and medications
support_anchor: Take medications
observable_conditions: Sleep and activity show a temporal relationship needing context
required_context: Substance and medication history for causal interpretation
non_applicable_conditions: Assuming unrecorded exposures occurred

title: Resting heart rate is measured in a resting context
content: Google describes resting heart rate as beats per minute while still and well rested. A daily resting estimate is different from an instantaneous exercise heart rate.
source_locator: Track your resting heart rate; Understand resting heart rate
support_anchor: still and well-rested
observable_conditions: Resting heart rate observations are available
non_applicable_conditions: Substituting exercise heart rate for resting heart rate

title: Daily resting and sleeping heart rates are different
content: Google explains that sleeping heart rate is measured throughout the night and is often lower than the daily resting estimate. Trends should compare the same measure rather than interchange these two values.
source_locator: How is resting heart rate different from sleeping heart rate
support_anchor: different from sleeping heart rate
observable_conditions: A daily resting heart-rate trend is being interpreted
required_context: The heart-rate measure and collection context are known
non_applicable_conditions: Mixing sleeping and resting heart-rate series

title: Several factors can influence resting heart rate
content: Google lists caffeine, alcohol, stress, fever, temperature, medicines, and regular exercise among influences on resting heart rate. A rise has several possible explanations and does not identify its cause.
source_locator: Know the factors that affect resting heart rate
support_anchor: Several factors can affect resting heart rate
observable_conditions: Resting heart rate changes relative to the person's previous readings
required_context: Exposure or symptom information to attribute a cause
non_applicable_conditions: Inferring stress, infection, or medication use from a rise alone

title: HRV measures variation between beats
content: Google describes heart-rate variability as variation in the time between heartbeats. HRV is not the same quantity as average heart rate, even when both are reported for the same sleep period.
source_locator: Understand each vital; Heart Rate Variability
support_anchor: variation in time between heartbeats
observable_conditions: HRV and heart-rate estimates are being interpreted together
non_applicable_conditions: Treating HRV as average heart rate

title: HRV depends on personal and lifestyle context
content: Google notes that HRV differs between people and is influenced by age, sleep, circadian rhythm, and lifestyle. One person's absolute HRV should not be treated as a universal normal value.
source_locator: Understand each vital; Heart Rate Variability
support_anchor: HRV varies from person to person
observable_conditions: An HRV level or trend is being reviewed
required_context: Personal history and consistent measurement context
non_applicable_conditions: Universal diagnosis from an HRV number

title: Personal ranges provide recent-trend context
content: Google calculates a personal range for each vital using up to thirty days of recent data to help monitor trends. A change relative to personal history is different from a comparison between people.
support_anchor: based on up to 30 days of data
observable_conditions: A vital has changed from a recent personal baseline
non_applicable_conditions: A single isolated reading without history

title: Follow resting heart rate over more than one day
content: Google's app provides resting-heart-rate views over weeks and months, including period averages. Reviewing repeated readings preserves trend context that a single daily estimate cannot provide.
source_locator: Check your resting heart rate; In the Google Health app
support_anchor: view heart rate trends over time
observable_conditions: Repeated resting heart-rate readings or a recent change
non_applicable_conditions: Concluding a persistent trend from one reading

title: HRV trends are wellness observations, not diagnoses
content: Google's vitals feature, which includes HRV, provides information for well-being and is not intended to diagnose or treat a medical condition. An observed HRV change alone therefore does not identify a disease.
source_locator: Understand vitals and Manage your data and privacy settings
support_anchor: not intended to diagnose or treat any medical condition
observable_conditions: An HRV trend is available for wellness monitoring
non_applicable_conditions: Diagnosing stress, anxiety, infection, or other disease from HRV

title: Fitbit reports HRV using RMSSD
content: Google specifies the RMSSD formula for Fitbit HRV. Comparisons should preserve the reported metric definition rather than assume every quantity called HRV is interchangeable.
source_locator: How does my Fitbit device track HRV
support_anchor: Root mean square of successive differences
observable_conditions: HRV records identify RMSSD as their metric
non_applicable_conditions: Comparisons with an unidentified HRV metric

title: The overnight HRV collection period matters
content: Google's Fitbit HRV estimate comes from the longest sleep period in the previous twenty-four hours; only periods longer than three hours are considered. This is device-specific collection guidance.
source_locator: How does my Fitbit device track HRV
support_anchor: longest sleep period over the past 24 hours
observable_conditions: Overnight HRV estimates or missing HRV are being compared
required_context: Compatible Fitbit collection definition and sleep coverage
non_applicable_conditions: Applying this rule universally to other devices

title: Sleep stage patterns naturally vary across nights
content: Google advises reviewing sleep-stage patterns over time rather than focusing on one day and offers comparison with a personal thirty-day average. This concerns sleep-stage data, which simple duration records do not contain.
support_anchor: rather than focusing too much on any one day
observable_conditions: Sleep-stage data vary between nights
non_applicable_conditions: Only sleep duration and timing are available

title: Health concerns require a clinical conversation
content: Google directs users with health concerns about vitals to a healthcare provider. Wellness readings can support that conversation but do not independently identify a condition or authorize treatment.
source_locator: Introduction and Manage your data and privacy settings
support_anchor: For health concerns, consult a healthcare provider
observable_conditions: A person reports concerns about a vital trend
non_applicable_conditions: Declaring an emergency from a relative trend without clinical context

title: Sensor fit influences heart-rate accuracy
content: Google says heart-rate accuracy depends on physiology, placement, and activity. The device should contact the skin with a snug, comfortable band; poor fit can affect an apparent change.
source_locator: Improve the accuracy of your heart rate reading
support_anchor: device placement on your arm
observable_conditions: Heart-rate readings may be unreliable or wear quality changes
non_applicable_conditions: Assuming fit problems when no evidence exists

title: Night-time coverage is required for overnight vitals
content: Google recommends wearing the device during the day and during sleep when troubleshooting missing vitals. Daytime wear alone does not demonstrate that an overnight metric was captured.
support_anchor: during the day and to sleep at night
observable_conditions: Overnight vitals have missing readings or uncertain coverage
non_applicable_conditions: Using daytime coverage as proof of overnight validity

title: Missing vitals can reflect inadequate sleep data
content: Google notes that most vitals require at least three hours of quality sleep and may be missing when a session is too short or movement excessive. Missing readings are not physiological zero values.
support_anchor: Most metrics require at least 3 hours of quality sleep
observable_conditions: A vital is missing with limited night-time data
required_context: Compatible Google or Fitbit device and sleep coverage
non_applicable_conditions: Interpreting a missing measurement as zero

title: Device support and syncing affect data availability
content: Google advises checking syncing and whether the device supports a missing vital. Missing data can result from data availability rather than an actual change in the person's health.
support_anchor: Check if your Fitbit device or Pixel Watch synced recently
observable_conditions: Vitals are missing or delayed
non_applicable_conditions: Treating unsupported metrics as measured zeros

title: Sensor or algorithm changes affect cross-device comparisons
content: Google warns that heart-rate readings can differ between devices because of technology, sensor, or algorithm changes. A device switch may complicate a comparison with an earlier personal baseline.
source_locator: My heart rate readings are inconsistent between devices
support_anchor: changes in the heart rate sensor or algorithm
observable_conditions: Heart-rate series involve a device or algorithm change
non_applicable_conditions: Assuming a device switch in a documented same-device series

title: Estimated time asleep is different from the full sleep period
content: Google estimates time asleep from the portions of the main sleep period classified as light, deep, or REM sleep. Recorded bedtime-to-wake duration need not equal estimated minutes asleep.
source_locator: Review how Google Health app calculates time asleep
support_anchor: Your time asleep is estimated
observable_conditions: Device-estimated sleep duration and sleep boundaries are available
non_applicable_conditions: Treating estimated sleep as a clinical sleep study

title: Wear the tracker overnight for a sleep record
content: Google says wrist devices automatically detect sleep when worn to bed and recommends a snug wristband. An unworn night should remain a missing observation rather than be interpreted as no sleep.
source_locator: How Google Health automatically detects sleep
support_anchor: when you wear your device to bed
observable_conditions: Sleep readings are absent with non-wear or incomplete night-time coverage
non_applicable_conditions: Treating non-wear as zero sleep

title: Step counts depend on movement sensing and arm motion
content: Google states that Fitbit counts steps with an accelerometer and that arm swing is needed during walking or running. Changes in how the device is worn or used can affect recorded steps.
source_locator: How does my Fitbit device count steps taken; accuracy tips
support_anchor: Fitbit devices use a 3-axis accelerometer to count your steps
support_anchors: your arm must swing back and forth
observable_conditions: Step readings change with possible measurement limitations
non_applicable_conditions: Assuming low recorded steps always mean less actual walking
